newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr hounded to support by hostile crowd.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr hounded to support by hostile crowd.

text.p: The Australian dollar found itself cornered at crucial support in a tense Thursday session as bears chased it lower in the face of spirited exporter buying.

It again failed to draw more than momentary comfort from the fact the Reserve Bank did not pander to market whim and cut rates again. A bounce was cut off at the knees at US$0.7585 as U.S. investment houses and funds sold and the dollar spent the rest of the day uncomfortably close to key US$0.7550 support.
There were also signs of offers from Tokyo, which alarmed dollar supporters as Japanese investors had recently been nowhere near as aggressive sellers as their U.S. counterparts.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the local dollar was cornered at US$0.7575/80 having retreated from US$0.7690/95 late here Wednesday and a brief peak of US$0.7630.
Traders said stops were thought to be building below US$0.7550, the previous low for the year, and a break could well trigger a burst of distressed selling down to 75 cents.

That would also be very bearish from a technical viewpoint with analysts seeing US$0.7450 as a first target, and potential for the downtrend to reach the 1996 trough of 73 cents. A push atop US$0.7630 was needed to relieve the immediate pressure, and a reversal would only come with the seizure of US$0.7770.
On the crosses the currency slipped to 87.77/87 yen from 88.40/50 late Wednesday as those AUD/yen offers came out of Tokyo, and to 57.7 in trade weighted terms from 57.9.

The dollar did try to bounce after the Reserve Bank stayed silent at its morning market operation, again confounding speculation of an imminent easing, but the rally had hardly reached US$0.7585 before fresh selling emerged.

Some bulls were hoping today's inaction by the central bank meant rates were on hold until its next board meeting in July but conceded it was impossible for the market to relax given the bank had surprised with three of the last four cuts.
Dealers were hoping for some guidance on policy by RBA governor Ian Macfarlane who addresses a Westpac conference in London tonight at around 01.50 am our time.
No title for the speech was known but it was thought to be about economic developments in Australia, so some inkling of the bank's policy thinking may emerge.

Wednesday's March quarter GDP report failed to settle the rate question one way or the other and the market would have to wait for May employment data next Thursday for another economic signpost on policy.
